draft.title: Tides
card: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the ocean's level. High tide is when the water is at its highest and low tide is when it is at its lowest.
The moon's gravity pulls on the Earth's oceans. This pull makes the water bulge, which causes high tides. The sun's gravity also pulls on the oceans, but less, because the sun is much further away.
As the Earth turns, a place moves through the bulges and the lower water between them. This is why most coasts have high and low tides each day.
a tide with a very high high tide and a very low low tide. It happens when the sun and moon line up with the Earth, so their pulls add together. It has nothing to do with the season of spring.
draft.remember: Moon's gravity is the main cause of tides. When the sun and moon line up, the pulls add together to make spring tides.

a.q: What is the main cause of the ocean's tides?
opts: The pull of the moon's gravity on the oceans
The pull of the sun's gravity on the oceans
Winds blowing the water towards the coast
The Earth's tilt as it moves around the sun
a.why: The moon's gravity pulls on the oceans and makes the water bulge, which causes high tides. The sun's gravity also pulls, but it has less effect because the sun is much further away.
a.clue: Which object is closest to Earth and pulls hardest on the water?

b.q: At a beach in Broome, the sun, Earth and moon are lined up and the tide range is the biggest of the month. What type of tide is this?
opts: A spring tide, because the pulls add together
A spring tide, because it happens in the season of spring
A weak tide, because the pulls work against each other
A weak tide, because the sun's pull cancels the moon's
b.why: When the sun and moon line up with the Earth, their pulls add together. This makes a very high high tide and a very low low tide, called a spring tide. The name does not come from the season of spring.
b.clue: Think about what happens to two pulls in the same direction.

a.best: The pull of the moon's gravity on the oceans

b.best: A spring tide, because the pulls add together

problems.detail: The card says the sun's gravity pulls on the oceans 'less' than the moon's. This is false. The sun's gravitational pull on Earth is much stronger than the moon's. What is smaller is the sun's tide-raising effect, because that depends on the difference in pull across the Earth, which falls off sharply with distance. Reword it to say the sun has a smaller effect on tides because it is much further away.

The clue asks 'Which object is closest to Earth and pulls hardest on the water?' The moon does not pull hardest; the sun's gravitational pull is stronger. The moon has the bigger tidal effect. The clue teaches a misconception.

The clue says 'two pulls in the same direction'. Spring tides also happen at full moon, when the sun and moon are on opposite sides of Earth and their pulls point in opposite directions. The clue could mislead students into thinking spring tides happen only at new moon.
